summary:
Neuquén Province stands under Argentina's national framework: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. No Neuquén-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented. The province is classified among units with no sub-national signal, and that classification carries a standing caveat: most such provinces retain contravención or faltas powers, the police-infraction instrument an NGO survey holds responsible for most arrests of trans and travesti people. Absence of documentation therefore indicates no exposure.

Exposure for a visitor in Neuquén runs through the national instruments. The decree of 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender detainees in prisons; both apply in Neuquén as in every province. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention. The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

Violence nationally reached a documented peak in 2025. The national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes against LGBT+ people over the year, a rise of 62% year-on-year, one every 38 hours and the worst total in the observatory's ten years. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 of 227. In 64.8% of cases, 147, the harm was physical violence against bodily integrity, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, and the surge is attributed to the government's 'cultural battle' and hate discourse.

Institutional support has been withdrawn at federal level. President Javier Milei eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts and which activists say is no longer being implemented. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice, according to trans activists interviewed in April 2025, who described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with deterioration assessed against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's statutory position remains among the most permissive in the world on paper. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The country was also the first in Latin America to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

The gap between statute and enforcement is the operative risk factor. Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime total as an inflection point in violence against LGBT+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm, and trans activists in Buenos Aires representing organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Neuquén face the same federal retreat as the rest of the country: the elimination of the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, the non-implementation of the 1% Trans Labor Quota in public-sector hiring, and the dismissal of trans employees recruited under it. The Gender Identity Law continues to govern legal recognition for residents, but activists report that its guarantees are no longer backed by an implementing ministry.

Provincial anti-discrimination law forms part of the protection available to residents alongside national provisions. Day-to-day exposure for trans and travesti residents is shaped less by the Gender Identity Law than by provincial contravención and faltas powers, the police-infraction instrument an NGO survey identifies as responsible for most arrests of trans and travesti people, and by the presence of security-force personnel among the predominant perpetrators of recorded hate violence.

For minors, DNU 62/2025 and the decree of 5 February 2025 restrict access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and the second decree of that month determines where transgender detainees are housed in prisons. Both bind residents of Neuquén as they do those of every other province.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Neuquén-specific enforcement data, arrest series, hate-crime breakdown or incident record is sourced for this province, so the local picture is unresolved rather than assessed as low-risk. Whether Neuquén's own contravención or faltas code contains provisions bearing on gender expression, and how those powers have been used against trans and travesti people here, is not documented in the available inventory.

Not sourced: whether Neuquén operates a provincial anti-discrimination body or hate-crime reporting mechanism, how the prison-placement decree of February 2025 has been implemented in Neuquén's detention facilities, and whether the provincial judiciary has applied or declined the travesticidio aggravating circumstance. The 227 hate-crime figure for 2025 is a national total with no provincial attribution available, so Neuquén's share of that count is unknown.
